Mr. Speaker, I hope that people understand that the two minutes that you referred to are the two minutes that I spoke on this Bill in a particular debate, as before Christmas I spoke in this House, obviously, for much more than two minutes.
I am glad to be recognized to speak in this debate, but in a way it is sad because it follows the arbitrary action of the Government to impose closure on this debate. I suppose that the Government moved in that direction because the arguments that have been put forward from this side of the House are beginning to hit home and it is feeling the heat. The Government probably feels that if it allowed this debate to continue, it might feel the continuing pressure to withdraw this legislation and to change its policy of six and five as it applies to Family Allowances.
The legislation that is before us today, Bill C-132, the application of six and five to Family Allowances in this country, is fundamentally an attack on human dignity. I want to elaborate on that. It is an attack on human dignity in the sense that, first and foremost, six and five is the Government's economic policy. It is its contention that inflation is the most important problem in this country and it has demonstrated to everyone that fighting inflation is its priority. In other words, by the application of this six and five program, the Government has accepted continued unemployment for at least 1.5 million people. This figure is the official statistic of unemployment in this country. So having 1.5 million people unemployed has not yet moved this Government to make unemployment its
priority. It continues with its misguided efforts at wrestling inflation to the ground, and that is what six and five is all about. Fundamentally and effectively the Government has abandoned any notion of providing employment for everyone who wants and needs employment, and has abandoned the policy objective of full employment.
In these times that is a direct attack on human dignity, because every person has a basic need to engage in productive activity. In this society in which we live, the way we distribute revenue is through the employment that we have. In our society it is necessary to have a good income in order to live a decent life and sustain one's feelings of self-worth and dignity. Six and five, as an economic policy, places the priority on fighting inflation, downgrades the importance of employment and undermines the dignity which the average Canadian enjoys.
Unemployment not only hurts the person who is unemployed, it also hurts the person who has a job. It does that because everyone is insecure in their employment, and they live in fear. To live in fear is a very negative experience and adds in no way whatsoever to the quality of life in this country.
The reason I emphasize the employment aspect of six and five, when we are talking about Family Allowances, is that it is hard to understand what the Government is doing in applying six and five to Family Allowances. In the first instance what it appears to be doing is attacking the notion of universality in social programs. In other words, it has capped the increase of Family Allowances, which is a universal program which goes to every citizen in the country. In order to deflect criticism, the Government has added something to the Child Tax Credit, which is a selective program. It has made a fundamental choice to go with selective programs as opposed to universal programs.
The problem with that approach in the social policy field is that it is an attack on human dignity. I say that because we know that once programs start to move down the road of selectivity, once you have to prove that you are poor before you can get social benefits, these programs have attached to them a negative stigma which says that anybody who applies is less than an equal, less than the person who does not have to apply.
This is a retrograde step in terms of social policy in this country and a direct attack on the respect that each individual receives. This Bill needs to be withdrawn. It should be put in the ashcan. The Government has to come up with better social

February 8, 1983
Family Allowances Act, 1973
policies that go in the right direction, and with an effective economic policy.
One of the problems in moving this Government to withdraw this legislation is that the whole of the Opposition, the Official Opposition and the NDP Opposition in this House, are not united. The Progressive Conservative Party have taken two stands on the six and five program. That has made them ineffective in fighting this inhumane action by the Government.
When the six and five legislation first came out, the Tories voted for it. They moved in one direction. They did not seem to understand the implications of the six and five legislation, the fact that it places a priority on fighting inflation and downgrades the problems of unemployment. They did not seem to understand that this legislation would be applied to Family Allowances, old age pensions and Public Service pensions. When the specific legislation applying to Family Allowances came into the House, they reversed themselves and went in the other direction.
What message is the Government to take from that? It takes the message that the Official Opposition, the Tory Party, does not know what it is doing and cannot mount an effective attack against the Government, even though the legislation is inhumane.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-132, a Bill to amend the Family Allowances Act, is the third string in the Government's program to attack the poor people of Canada. Over the years the Government has built up these huge deficits which have led to the inflation which is now leading to the economic collapse in which we find ourselves, so people are having to cut back. We agreed with six and five as an over-all program to cut back in the future, but we certainly did not agree to the Government applying it in these specific areas. As you know, we opposed it when the Government tried to break contracts with retired federal civil servants, we opposed it with respect to the senior citizens, and we are opposing it with respect to the Family Allowances, because, Mr. Speaker, it is being applied unfairly.
As I mentioned before, the Minister herself, who receives $100,000 plus, will this year take an additional $6,500 out of the Canadian economy even though she is not working one bit harder than she was last year. We, as Members of Parliament, will be taking an additional $3,900 out of the economy in 1983, even though we are working not one bit harder than last year. Yet we expect the mothers receiving Family Allowances to take only 6 per cent when they had guaranteed to them full indexation. That is not fair, Mr. Speaker. It might seem like very little money, $17 per child per year, but that $17 to the mother who is barely at the poverty line is much more significant than the $3,900 is to you and me, because our actual cost of living has not gone up $3,900.
There is a solution, however. Had the Government been genuinely fair in treating Canadians, it would have brought in a law that said that rather than six and five, there would be a flat across-the-board payment-just to pick a figure, say,
February 8, 1983

$1,000 across the board. You and I would get $1,000 and that probably would cover our cost-of-living increase. Well, why not give that to the senior citizens, because their actual cost of living has gone up by that much?
I put that argument to the Minister a few days ago and she stood up with some response which was totally out of context. It was almost as if she did not understand the point I was making, which was that in times of hard inflation when we as a nation decide there has to be a cutback, the way to achieve that cutback is to give a flat across-the-board settlement of, say, $1,000 or $2,000. The people near the poverty line would then come up and those at the top would come down, and we as a society would get closer and closer together.
As I have argued before, the real effect of inflation where you have across-the-board settlements of 6 per cent or 10 per cent is that the rich become incredibly rich and the poor just barely inch up, so that as a Canadian society we get further and further apart. Surely during times of inflation we should be trying to come closer together, particularly when you are trying to adjust to the situation. That has been my argument, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I can stand with absolutely no hesitation and argue against the position of the New Democratic Party and say we are opposing this specific Bill even though we are in agreement with general restraint across the country. We can all agree on restraint. It is the application of it, where you have to decide whether or not you are being fair, that is important.
The NDP push this nation into huge deficits, Mr. Speaker, to the point where 25 per cent to 30 per cent of every tax dollar which comes into the federal Government now goes to service the debt. Where does that 30 per cent go? It goes to people who already have wealth. So when you build up deficits and top that with inflation, you get a concentration of wealth in the hands of people with money already, rather than the poor. That is the direct fall-out from the policies of deficit financing that we on this side have been arguing against for so many years.
1 will continue to say that again and again and again, Mr. Speaker, because Canadians are beginning to realize that the real problem is deficits. They lead to inflation as night follows day, and inflation, as day follows night, leads to economic collapse. It has happened time and time again throughout history, in Canada and in every other country in the world, and until Canadians come to realize that, take their sovereignty back, and real limits on the power of Governments to interfere in their lives, we will continue this circle through history.

It is clear, Mr. Speaker, to this side of the House that the Liberal Party has not won the battle against inflation. What it did was create such economic chaos that nobody could buy anything. It won the battle against inflation by creating the chaos and making it so no one could afford to buy. That certainly brings prices down because manufacturers are not manufacturing for inventory, they are clearing out inventory.

Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), put in an amendment to endeavour to stop this Government from carrying on ad nauseam with its decision to fight inflation, and then take credit for beating inflation on the backs of the poor families of Canada. I know that is the position of the Minister and the Government but we feel it is not fair to ask them to bear that burden. As a result of Liberal Government policies, more and more Canadian families are living at the poverty level. I am not sure whether that has ever been stated as firm Government policy, but it is certainly a firm happening in the country.
In my riding of Simcoe North there is 33 per cent unemployment in the Town of Midland as a result of the failure of the Government to react to economic circumstances throughout Canada and the world. Having created that chaos, that hardship and unemployment, the Government feels it will

Time and time again we have suggested that there are better ways to fight the battle. Member for Calgary West, which is made in good faith and would give the Government an opportunity to come to its senses on the capping of the indexation of Family Allowances. Members go back and look at the speeches made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) when she was debating the Bill which would bring about a tax benefit at the end of the year for families. At that time she said that they were the vulnerable ones. These people include housewives and mothers, single parents or others, in Canada. The Minister and other Members went on to say that this may be the only cheque that these people can cash if they are not single parents. The Government now says that it wants to cut

February 8, 1983

back on these cheques. When we debated the Child Tax Credit two years ago they were the vulnerable ones. Today they are expendable.
As I said at the outset, this legislation in its global sense is an attack on Canadian families, whether senior citizens, retired public servants or children. They are the ones the Government has chosen to bear the brunt of its attack on inflation.
1 support my colleague's amendment to terminate this six and five program at the end of 1983 because the Government's record has shown that it is a poor planner. It cannot predict what will happen in 1984. When we have three different budget projections in one year, all of them updated and upgraded to show that the Government deficit will be even larger than its previous estimate, I do not think the Government is qualified to make projections on the restriction of family incomes into 1984. Surely if it wants to operate according to its record, it should limit itself to the year we are in. Therefore, I support my colleague's amendment to limit this legislation to one year.
Last week 1 mentioned one illustration of the Government's inability to plan. In November, 1981 the Government floated a Canada Savings Bond at the incredible rate of 19 per cent plus. It raised $12 billion through that bond which could have been invested in the private sector. Since interest rates plummeted soon after that bond was floated, the Government paid out more than $2 billion in interest charges which should not have been paid as a result of the interest rates dropping. The Government borrows money on the New York bond market on a three-month term whereas it borrows on the Canada Savings Bond on a one-year term. The Government is not very competent in planning what its future costs will be.
I am in favour of this amendment because it is the Government that creates inflation by its expensive operations. We now have legislation before us which prohibits the taxpayer from protecting himself from the inflation that the Government itself creates. I consider that to be wrong.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in opposition to Bill C-132 and in support of the amendment moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). We on this side of the House have no illusions about the result of this amendment. We know that it cannot make the Bill any more acceptable to the Canadian people, but it can go a long way to offset the damage that will be created by this Bill once it is passed by the Government.
As the Member for St. Catharines, I want to say that I am naturally very much concerned about unemployment and the poor state of the economy that exists in the St. Catharines and Niagara region. St. Catharines-Niagara has the highest rate of urban unemployment in this country. One out of every five workers is unemployed. Jobs have disappeared at the rate of 1,750 a month over the last two years.
We now have Bill C-132. We have heard many irrelevant speeches and comments from those on the Government side of the House. They say that we in the Opposition are making a mountain out of a molehill. Let me offset this argument which Government Members tend to make. We hear them ask what
Family Allowances Act, 1973
difference does it make? We hear them say that any mother should be prepared to contribute this part of her income to the six and five program by having her Family Allowance cheque reduced from $30 per month to $28.52 per month. Is that a hardship?
The response is quite simple. In the City of St. Catharines alone the loss in 1983 will amount to over $50,000 a month, and this amount will be compounded each month during the time the recipient receives the benefit. That represents nothing less than a one-year tax increase of $600,000 applied to over 22,000 families in St. Catharines, almost 25 per cent of which are single parent families.
What is even more reprehensible, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that we are not talking about wealthy families. According to Revenue Canada, the average person living in St. Catharines is earning just over $13,000 a year. The single parent trying to raise a child or children on $13,000 a year is hardly in a position to join the war against this Government's inflation. That parent is already waging a personal war without needing to do double duty on behalf of a Government that keeps spending.
The Government knows this. According to the 1981 edition of taxation statistics, St. Catharines' taxpayers paid annually an average of $3,000 each to the federal Government. In the 1982 edition, that average is down to $2,265, a drop of almost 25 per cent. Indeed, on a total net tax paid basis, and taking inflation into account, the federal Government's revenues from the City of St. Catharines has dropped by $3.4 million in just one year. This reflects the staggering rate of unemployment in our area and the poor state of the region's economy. Yet it tells a good deal more than that. It tells us that the federal Government is losing revenue from the St. Catharines' people; and this Bill, along with the attack on old age pensioners in Bill C-131, is simply a further attempt at a tax grab.
In committee, witness after witness made the point that this Bill will hurt low-income earners the most and wealthy Canadians the least. It was further pointed out that if the Government were serious about being socially and economically responsible, then tax reform was the route to follow.
Several excellent suggestions were made with respect to the Child Tax Credit, the Family Allowance Program and the tax exemption for dependants. The thrust of these suggestions was to the effect that the Government could do far more for women in general, could do more for middle-income families in particular, while not increasing expenditures and indeed would have the opportunity to cut costs.
The Government's response was typical of its attitude, an attitude that has prevailed since the 1980 election. This is our Bill, the Government says. This is the way it is, and that is the way it is going to be, is what we hear. Only one amendment has been adopted since debate began on these last three six and five Bills. That amendment was granted under threat of revolt

February 8, 1983
Family Allowances Act, 1973
from Liberal backbenchers, and under the threat of closure with respect to each.
Efforts on the part of the Opposition to reduce the damage that will be inflicted by those Bills have been rewarded by a series of closure motions to cut off debate and discussion of the responsible approach to pension and taxation reform. In the case of this Bill, the Government did not even wait for the call of closure or for the axe of fall. Mothers had their January cheques reduced despite the fact that the legislation has not yet been passed. If the Government can thumb its nose at the law, then why should Canadians respect the law? Why should Canadians have trust and confidence in this Government? Why bother with the parliamentary process at all if this is the way the Government chooses to operate? Give a Bill first reading, make a few remarks and send everybody home. When will this Government respect the fact that Canadian expect their Parliament to operate in a spirit of co-operation and compromise? What we have today is rule by closure and by order in council.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), has put forward an amendment that deserves this Government's support. We will be watching in what numbers, if any, Government backbenchers will rise in support of this amendment. It is an amendment that limits the application of this Bill to one year and gives the Government an opportunity to reassess its approach and see what impact the legislation will have in that one year. Over that period of a year the Government may realize that the Bill has no economic merit, no economic impact and that it is socially regressive. Conversely, the Government may even regard the program as pure genius and wish to extend it if that can be justified. But that decision cannot be made now.
A lot can happen during 1983. To legislate for 1984 on the basis of the Government's guesstimates is completely irresponsible. We are not talking about an insignificant decision. We are not talking about an insignificant amount. Should inflation again reach astronomical heights in the last quarter of 1983 as it did in prior years, even in the months just gone by, mothers are condemned to getting by with 5 per cent protection in 1984. Surely to goodness, no Government would want to lay the foundation to such a dreadful scenario at the feet of the people of Canada, or expect that to happen and expect it to be accepted.
There is a second advantage to my colleague's amendment. This amendment takes into account the Government's own estimate or guesses about inflation. Canadians know perfectly well that inflation will not be the number one problem in 1983 or 1984. Unemployment and economic recovery have to get top priority. This amendment allows the Government to get on with that instead of fighting an ongoing battle against a third-ranked contender.
I intend to support this amendment, Mr. Speaker. If Members sitting in Government benches are in the least concerned with unemploment and with social progress, they too will support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to take part in this debate and to say at the outset that we too support the amendment put forward by the Official Opposition, but we are still fundamentally opposed to the whole Bill.
I have been here a number of years and this is the most outrageous effort at what I call nothing more than chiselling by the Government of all the efforts and times that I have seen this Government chisel here and there from those who can least defend themselves and from those who are most in need.
We saw an occurrence on Tuesday of last week in which the Government said it was prepared to provide hundreds of millions of dollars each year to our two national railways. The two national railways would be given hundreds of millions of dollars, and would be allowed a 39.5 per cent profit annually. I do not know of anyone who makes that kind of profit. Usually a reasonable return on investment is somewhere in the 10 per cent or 20 per cent area. Any Government which can find revenues to hand out to our two national railways and allow them to make that kind of unconscionable profit and at the same time chisel a few dollars a month from old age pensioners, Public Service retirees, Armed Forces retirees and children, surely must be some kind of obscenity. Any Government that can do that must have its priorities in reverse.
The Government, starting this year and continuing over the next several years, is prepared to spend $8 billion on a fighter plane which will be of little or no use to us, which will maximize profits for its manufacturers, and which will continue to escalate the arms race, but it cannot find a few dollars a month for the old, for retired public servants, for retired members of the Armed Forces, and for children. Surely that is an additional obscenity. All the Government has proven is that the money is there for these sorts of things, for unconscionable profittaking, not making, and military equipment, but it is not there for those who need it the most.
Many of these social payments in the form of pensions, the Family Allowance and so on, are taxable. Therefore, for those in the upper middle and high income groups, the Government will tax back most, all or even more than the increases provided for Family Allowances, for old age pensioners and retired public servants. It really is not a cost to the Government for those who do not necessarily need these increases. One way or another, the Government gets it back, and then some. It is generally efficiently administered. It is a simple way of maintaining universality and seeing to it that those who need it most get it and get to keep it. Surely it is no way to fight inflation on the backs of those who not only did not cause inflation, but are also its first victims.

Mr. Speaker, as a part of the six and five restraint program, the Family Allowances Act will set the monthly Family Allowance payments at 106 per cent of the 1982 level in 1983, and 105 per cent of the 1983 level in 1984. Monthly Family Allowance payments, which are currently $26.91 per child, will rise to $28.52 in 1983, and to $29.95 in 1984, a very small measure for the inflation that will probably be taking place. Had full indexing continued in 1983, average monthly payments per child would be some $30 at the rate of 11.5 per cent, and some $33 in 1984 at the same rate.
For most low and middle income families, this loss will be more than offset in 1983 by the one-year temporary increase of $50 per child in the Child Tax Credit program. But what happens in 1984? We have a Government Act which is to continue in force for two years and we are only offsetting it for the first year. That is why we require the amendment. The net result of this action of enriching the Child Tax Credit and partially deindexing Family Allowances is that the Government will spend more than $95 million more than it would have spent if neither program had been changed.
The Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) moved this amendment that we are now debating on the basis that he felt, and I agree, that it is impossible to predict just what inflation will be like in 1984, and therefore to project the program that far ahead was unfair to families. He also stated that the Bill should not be passed in the first place because of its attack on the Family Allowance, which is something which mothers in particular use in planning their budgets each month.
Family Allowance was initially introduced to help families or single parents raise their children. The mother always had a certain amount of money which she could set aside through the Family Allowance to provide the basic physical needs for her children. Why change that?

However, the battle against this much talked about enemy must start with those who are responsible for it, not mothers and children but Government. We must address the problems as they exist. I thought that perhaps the reason for this legislation is that this kind of suffering is an academic exercise for most Hon. Members opposite. They do not fully understand what impact this legislation can have on the 22,000 children in my constituency and the households across the nation. The impact can be severe indeed.
Let me go back to olden times, Mr. Speaker. I remember when I was living on a pittance and had two young children to support. I was attending university, which also explains why my income was so low. It became necessary for me to return to the university each evening to study. At that time the bus fare cost a dime. It took a total reshuffling of the family budget to clear that ten cents for the bus fare. The baby bonus cheque came once a month and helped with clothes for the two children and actually bought a little cheese for the macaroni that we seemed to have about three times a week. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I can sympathize with the thousands of families who live that way today with not much hope for a better life.
All this legislation will do is cause hardship. Hon. Members opposite may not think a few dollars a month is important, but to the family on welfare or on unemployment insurance trying to meet mortgage payments, this is a severe blow and is going to cause a great deal of hardship. Many families will have to reshuffle what is already an inadequate budget.
We are living in a world where the dynamics of social life are changing. The number of one-breadwinner families decreases each year. There are millions of women and men who prefer to see at least one parent available to the children for more time than they have available at present. I have knocked at most doors in my part of the world. Nothing is more tragic than when a seven year old sick little kid comes to the door because it is absolutely necessary for both the father and mother to work. There are thousands of such cases.
I hold no brief for those who say that women should stay at home. I do not accept that. If a woman wants a career she should have it, but if she has a child she has a strong responsibility, as does the husband. Sometimes we overlook that.
There is another phenomenon in the dynamics of social life that is changing. Many men would prefer to be a house husband and stay home to fill that traditional role.
This legislation indicates a philosophy that holds the family not to be important. It indicates an encouragement to force more women or men to go out and work who perhaps realize that the greatest contribution they can make is to the next generation, to their own children or to their neighbour's children. But we do not encourage that.
I wonder if the Minister has ever considered that this kind of philosophical legislation means that we will spend a lot more money in other areas of social responsibility. More funds will
February 8, 1983

be needed to help the broken home, the kid who goofs off and does not get an education, the street people on Davey Street in Vancouver or Yonge Street in Toronto. All of them came from homes that in one way or another were unsatisfactory.
How can we expect someone to go to work at eight o'clock in the morning, spend a heavy day there, come home at five o'clock in the afternoon and, even jointly, prepare dinner, look after a couple of kids, read a bedtime story, put them to bed properly and listen to their problems? For someone who is tired or had the kind of day at the office that the typical Member of this House has, that is hard to do.
The Government should be doing anything it can to help parents raise their children properly. It should realize the kinds of social problems that exist, rather than contributing to problems, as this legislation will.
We might look at what has happened in Sweden. Many families there share a job, one working at it for a few days and then the other, or perhaps one works half time and then the other one works half time. If the Government could make arrangements for two mothers each to work half time on a job, it could save the money that is now being spent in the courts of the country and would help with the broken lives of the young people that one can see on any street corner of our major cities.
When we talk to these kids we find that they did not get along at home for one reason or another. It is not because they are horrible little brats of 18 or 19 but, rather, because when they were three, four or five years of age there was nobody to listen to them or to talk to them. After a long day's work the parents were so tired they could not give the attention and love that a child is entitled to and deserves. We cannot afford to continue with this kind of improper social policy. We must find the money for good programs which are so important to people.
On behalf of the 22,000 youngsters in my riding and on behalf of their mothers and fathers, I ask the Liberal Government to please reconsider and withdraw this terrible piece of legislation. The Government just has to ask any Member of the Conservative Party and he will show where millions of dollars could be saved without affecting the homes and the young people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in debate on the amendment proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). I take very seriously indeed the Government's six and five program as it relates to three important sectors of our economy and three very important groups of people in our society, namely, the senior citizen, the pensioner who contributed to the security he hoped to enjoy after retirement, and the children of our nation.
I want to say that I take this issue most seriously because all of us, as Members of Parliament, have had the daily experience of receiving representations in our constituency office from those people who have been severely affected by the
Family Allowances Act, 1973
recession in Canada. They have asked us the simple question of what we as Members of Parliament can do and how we can help and advise them in terms of the negative effects they are feeling because of unemployment and the devalued dollar. I stand to participate in this debate because I have seen the strategy of this Government invoking a motion, whether it wants to call it time allocation or closure, to limit debate on legislation which affects the most important segment of our society.
One has to ask why this callous and arrogant attitude has been adopted by the Liberal Party. Why do we see the spectacle today of the Liberal Members sitting mute in their place and not saying anything in support of this legislation? While I am not casting any reflection or alleging any motivation on the part of Members of the Liberal Party, I think their silence indicates why we have seen this strategy adopted by the Government. The Government House Leader has realized the embarrassment and humiliation felt by every Member in the backbenches of the Liberal Party.
Those Members do not have any basis on which to stand and support this retrograde step in terms of the children or our nation. Indeed, the political consequences to each of them is known. They know that to stand up and attempt to defend the indefensible will cause them serious problems in the next election. It is in their own self-interest that they sit there and do not address this issue as to why we should support this particular proposal.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) herself has tried to skate around the issue by saying that we should not worry because this measure is merely symbolic. What kind of Alice in Wonderland are we seeing? The Minister of National Health and Welfare is charged with a statutory obligation to the children of this nation and their parents to see that there is no erosion of benefits paid to the children and parents of this country. For her to stand in her place and say that this is merely symbolic is not, I suggest, in the best traditions of ministerial responsibility.
When I think of the original principles of Liberalism in this country, those principles of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Right Hon. Mackenzie King who introduced this particular concept of Family Allowance in our country, I think of how they must be rolling and whirling in their graves to see these Liberals stand up and attack the very fabric and basis of what I call a truly Liberal policy and proposal with respect to support for those in our society who most need help.
I say to those Members of the Liberal Party who are sitting there and have supported these measures that whatever your rationale is, the people of Canada instinctively know-that you have deserted the traditions of Liberalism with your support of this kind of legislation. I merely want to say to those Members of the Liberal Party who are keeping silent and not participating in the debate that I recall that at your last annual meeting one resolution that received unanimity was one declaring that the Liberal Party abhors backroom, political manipulation in

subtopic: FACILITIES AT WOOD'S HARBOUR, N.S.
FACILITIES AT WOOD'S HARBOUR, N.S.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 want to call to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) the concern expressed by my constituents who are involved in the Fishery, a primary industry that is crumbling under the heavy hand of the present Liberal administration. A prime example is the plea made by the fishermen of Wood's Harbour, Shelburne County, where expanded harbour facilities are urgently required.
In 1982 the Small Craft Harbours Branch gave this requirement a "top priority" rating, yet as recently as January 20, 1983, the Minister informed me construction is not expected to commence until early in the 1984-1985 fiscal year, depending on other priorities and availability of funds.
How does the Minister of Fisheries reconcile this further delay in light of the statement made by his Department officials over three years ago, namely, that the expanded facilities at Wood's Harbour qualified for a "top priority" rating based on need. For the sake of the safety of the entire fleet, this work should be proceeded with immediately.

subtopic: IMPACT OF ENERGY TAXES ON PRODUCERS
IMPACT OF ENERGY TAXES ON PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my statement concerns the effects of federal energy taxes on the agricultural industry in Alberta. These concerns have been properly drawn to my attention by the Federation of Alberta Gas Co-ops Limited which supplies heat and energy to over 170,000 rural Albertans, with a 50,000 miles of distribution system.
Energy taxes have a very negative impact on basic agricultural production costs, such as fertilizers, chemicals, plastics, and many other materials made from a natural gas base, and make up 75 per cent of the total cost of nitrogen fertilizers. Increased costs for natural gas feedstock have raised the price of nitrogen fertilizer by 41 per cent over the last two years. Presently in Canada about 5 per cent of our population grows enough food to satisfy most of our own requirements, plus providing nearly $9 billion in export commodities.
The federal Government is placing too much of the burden of energy taxation on agricultural producers who should not be sacrificed for the sake of energy excise taxes. Very visible evidence of this sacrifice has been the recent decision to close, indefinitely, Western Co-Operative Fertilizer Ltd. in Medicine Hat, after 27 years of existence. About 100 permanent jobs are affected.

subtopic: CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF CHARGES AGAINST INDIANS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF CHARGES AGAINST INDIANS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, fisheries management and conservation require a good working relationship between the Department of Fisheries and all user groups, including the traditional Indian food fishery. On January 12 federal fisheries people destroyed this relationship when they arrested 130 people on charges of illegally selling fish. All but one of these people were native Indians. Obviously a method of entrapment had been used that discriminated against Indian people. The presence of television cameras in the pre-dawn raid gave the whole situation an obscene carnival atmosphere.
There are many victims of this stupid action-first, the 129 Indian people who were entrapped and arrested; second, all

February 8, 1983
Indian people in British Columbia who are trying to establish their aboriginal rights in the fishing industry; third, Department of Fisheries personnel who must continue to work in a deteriorating situation with Indian people and, fourth, all Canadians who care about conservation and fisheries management.
The Minister has recognized his mistake. I now call upon the Government to drop all charges against Indian fishermen based on entrapment. The Minister of Fisheries must begin to rebuild relationships with the Indian people by involving them in basic decisions regarding the conservation and management of our fisheries.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL AID-EFFECT ON NEWFOUNDLAND AND QUEBEC CARRIERS
GOVERNMENT FINANCIAL AID-EFFECT ON NEWFOUNDLAND AND QUEBEC CARRIERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to a situation that is unacceptable and that, in my opinion, requires corrective action as soon as possible. I am referring to the case of Atlantic Container Express, a marine transportation company in Newfoundland and Quebec, which is facing serious financial problems as a result of financial support being given by the Canadian Government to CN railways in Newfoundland.
Since 1979, the survival of a number of carriers has been threatened by the actions of Terra Transport, an operational division that takes care of the Newfoundland railway network. In fact, as a result of CN's financial support for this railway, rates have dropped by from 20 to 30 per cent, thus making this means of transportation more attractive than that offered by marine carriers. These rates are entirely non-compensatory. This policy is therefore harming marine shipping companies which are trying to compete however they can. For instance, Atlantic Container Express, a marine carrier which provides a service between Toronto and Newfoundland and between Montreal and Newfoundland has now lost part of its market because of unfair competition by CN.
Madam Speaker, I would therefore urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to bear in mind that the National Transportation Act provides that when Government support for a carrier proves harmful to another carrier in the private sector, immediate action must be taken.

HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT RATE IN GASPE

Madam Speaker, yesterday I described to the House the economic situation in the Gaspe. subtopic: MACDONALD ROYAL COMMISSION
MACDONALD ROYAL COMMISSION
subsubtopic: REMUNERATION OF CHAIRMAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister who, on a number of occasions, has asked Canadians to restrain their salary and wage demands and, where possible, in federal Government circles, to restrain their demands to six and five. He has asked the mothers of Canada to accept only a 6 per cent increase in Family Allowances this year, and less next year.
Having now been informed that his Government will be paying Donald Macdonald the obscene sum $800 a day, plus expenses, which is more money than the 2.3 million pensioners receive in Canada for an entire month, will the Prime Minister explain to this House and to the people of Canada how he can justify paying a certain individual $800 a day when he is not prepared to pay that same amount for a total month's income to a typical pensioner in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MACDONALD ROYAL COMMISSION
subsubtopic: REMUNERATION OF CHAIRMAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must explain to the Hon. Member that in effect all the Commissioners will be receiving remuneration possibly worth the same to all of them, something in the area of $350 a day.
The $800 is paid to the firms of three lawyers who are on the Commission, two lawyers are commissioners and one is a research assistant, and more than 50 per cent of those amounts will be retained by the firms to cover the overhead that each individual member of a firm must pay in order to be a partner of the firm. So in effect all the Commissioners will be receiving approximately the same amount, $350 a day, which is the usual amount paid in recent times to members of Royal Commissions.

subtopic: REASON FOR LEVEL OF REMUNERATION

Madam Speaker, I still believe this really does add insult to injury. Many Canadians believe that this three-year "Ronald McDonald" approach to economic planning is not needed in the first place. Now we find that we are going to be paying the participants such extravagant sums of money during these times which the Government is calling times of restraint.
I want to ask the Prime Minister, now that he has decided to pay Mr. Macdonald the sum of money that he has indicated, would it not be appropriate at least to expect a commitment from Mr. Macdonald that he will remain for three years, during the time of the inquiry, or is this the Prime Minister's way of extending the golden touch to the man he would like to see replace himself, instead of John Turner?

speechtext: I want to ask the Prime Minister if in fact this exorbitant salary is going to be paid to Mr. Macdonald, and to all the Commissioners appointed by the Prime Minister, which amount would allow 2,000 Canadians to have extended unemployment insurance benefits for a month, or 10,000 families to have fully indexed Family Allowances for one year, how, morally speaking, he can justify this kind of salary. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: JUSTIFICATION FOR REMUNERATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member's argument seems to turn on whether the Commission is necessary or not. If he does not agree with the figures that I have just quoted, that is a matter of judgment. I just put it that that is the information that I received from the Commission, and the information which has been made public and which can be tested against recent surveys by actuaries who do say that in fact more than 50 per cent of fees received by lawyers go to pay the overhead of their offices. That is another matter.
Assuming that the information is right, the question is, do we need a Royal Commission on Canada's economic future? My deep belief and that of, I would say, many members of the public and of the informed thinking critics of the Government, is that it is time that Canadians have a Royal Commission, outside of the day-to-day preoccupations of Governments and Oppositions, to look at Canada's future, to look at the structure of governments in this country and to see whether Canada's economic future can be improved both by economic means and by constitutional or political reform to institutions.
This is a serious question. I am surprised that the Opposition do not think that it is important because, when they were the Government, the then Leader of the Government, the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead, had proposed the setting up of such a commission. When the same Party are in opposition, they suddenly realize that no knowledge is better than some knowledge, which is not surprising coming from the Conservative Party.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I had just started the list, but I will stop here. It is a serious question. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CHAIRMAN'S FEES FROM DIRECTORSHIPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when one sets up a Royal Commission and one goes to members of the private sector to staff and fill the position of commissioners, one does it precisely because the interest and activities of the members of the private sector qualify them for the type of knowledge that will be needed to conduct a commission. If we did not want people with private sector interests, we would not go to the private sector to hire them. I have not heard the argument from the Hon. Member that to be a member of a Board of Directors of a company or to be a lawyer in a firm which is practising corporate law in the normal way disqualifies one from giving good advice to the Government on economic and constitutional matters.
Once again, if one wants to hire people from the private sector, one should take them with their knowledge, capacity, and with their activities. Otherwise one would have an inhouse Royal Commission staffed by public servants whose conflicts of interest are defined by the law.

First, can the Minister clarify what assistance the Canadian Government has offered those people who are dislocated, and secondly, has the Canadian Government protested to Nigeria for taking this precipitous action as a consequence of the international economic situation, on the grounds that it is a precedent for other countries creating economic refugees in order to deal with their own internal economic problems?

Madam Speaker, I should tell the Hon. Member we have made an initial contribution of $100,000 to the International Red Cross. We have provided an additional $30,000 to assist in the transport of milk powder. We are now receiving an assessment from international organizations and we are prepared to consider short-term relief for the persons expelled from Nigeria to Ghana, and also a program of longer term assistance.
I understand that, in my absence, the Minister of State for International Trade expressed the concern of the Government of Canada to the Nigerian High Commissioner about this particularly rapid request to these persons to leave the country. speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-132, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs; and the motion of Mr. Hawkes (p. 21697).

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, during the two minutes when I spoke before the luncheon adjournment, I was interrupted by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) on a point of order. It was not a point of order according to the ruling of the Chair, and in addition to that the Hon. Minister was completely in error. He said that on this side we were having difficulty getting speakers. Perhaps we should look at the record. This morning alone there were ten Progressive Conservative speakers but not one Member of the Government stood up to be recognized. That is a ratio of ten to none. In this entire debate only three Members of the Liberal Party have spoken, apart from the Minister and her Parliamentary Secretary. Of course, they have to be here to support the Bill; indeed, they have no choice but to support it. But only three other Members of the Liberal Party have stood to support it, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Collenette), the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) and the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster).
There is a long list of Progressive Conservatives and New Democratic Party Members who oppose taking bread out of the mouths of the children of this country, but it is sad that Members of the Government do not even stand up to support the Bill. But, when the time comes for the vote, however, no doubt they will vote for this legislation, which should have been withdrawn weeks ago.
February 8, 1983

Let us look at some of the facts in connection with the legislation. The Minister said that there are about 3.6 million mothers who receive the Family Allowance and then said that the indexation will not affect two-thirds of them. That leaves
1.200.000	mothers whose indexation will be affected. It is like the man who looks at a bottle of whiskey and says that it is half empty. The Minister says no, it is half full. There are
1.200.000	mothers who will be affected by this legislation.
Do Hon. Members realize what havoc that will cause to the great majority of those families? While some do not need the Family Allowance, each family decides how to use that benefit. Family Allowance was a declared policy in this country so that young people would have an income of their own that would be sent to the mother or the father. It was to be used for the benefit of these boys and girls. Every family has used the money in different ways.
One family I know has put that money faithfully into a trust account each month. When their children reach 18 there will be money available to send them to university or college. That family has made excellent use of the Family Allowance. Their children will receive a better education and make a better contribution to the country.
Other families must use their Family Allowance to keep bread on the table. When I was in high school I did not like returning on the first day of school, not because it was not wonderful meeting my friends after the summer vacation, but it was the day when children were given a list of books to buy.
I hated the thought of going home with that list of books that we could illafford to buy. We had a large family and at that time the mines were not operating. There was no Family Allowance or other income coming in and we had to stretch our money in order to keep bread on the table. My mother went without food very often in order that the children could have something to eat. However, when I showed this list of books that I needed to buy, they found a way to scrape the money together so that I could get through school. Sometimes I would borrow books until we were able to buy them, and occasionally it was the end of October before I could get them all. Fortunately, I had understanding teachers who knew I could not afford the books, but through the sacrifice of my brothers and sisters and my parents I eventually got them.
Parents who are sending their children to colleges and universities today are faced with a great problem. They must buy books and clothes for their children. There are also tuition fees and other fees at particular colleges or universities, as well as for room and board. These expenses cause great worry to the parents in this country. Now their Family Allowances may be cut. This will affect those children in high school and those who enter university before they are 18 because their future education will be jeopardized. In other words, the future of our young people is being affected by this legislation.
If the Government needs money, I can think of a dozen better ways to get it than taking it from the young people of this country who are the future of this nation. Our young
Family Allowances Act, 1973
people should be encouraged to get an education, but this measure will only encourage them to quit school and try to get a job since it will be difficult for their parents to supply their books, clothing and other needs.
Young people are proud. When I went to school many boys wore long trousers when they went to high school. I did not get a pair of long trousers until I got to grade 12. I was embarrassed many times because I did not have long trousers like the other kids. I came from a mining camp and others came from the east end of Drumheller, but I always had sympathy and help at home.
This Government is telling mothers that it will not longer give them this allowance. It will take away an average of $17 per child over a year. That $17 is enough to buy three or four of the books that the child needs. It is enough to buy milk for the baby. Some may say "What is $17?". I remember when I thought $1 was an awful lot of money. I remember the time when I wished that I had 25 cents in my pocket. That $17 does not sound like much when one receives a big salary, like $800 a 'day for Mr. Macdonald. Incidentally, he will not even pay his own expenses. He will get $125 to eat out at the Imperial Room, of course, not at the greasy spoon down the street where many others have to eat.
This Bill is completely wrong because it attacks the wrong people. If we need the money, why do we not take it from some of the Government's advertising budget? I received a letter today from an editor of the Cochrane Times. She asked me what the cost of all this advertising was. She said that she was throwing these advertisements into the wastepaper basket. Here it is, a fancy card in big envelopes. These are being mailed out to many people. I suggest that not even one out of 200 stop to read it.
Furthermore, the Government has set up this Law Reform Commission. Has the Government yet followed one precept that this committee has recommended? The committee has only made recommendations, which is misleading. People will think that this is the law but it is not. It is only what the commission thinks should be the law. While the Government spends thousands of dollars on this type of document, it is taking the bread out of the mouths of the kids in order to keep the Government operating. It is a shameful act by this Government.
I see you are indicating that I have one minute left Mr. Speaker. I am almost through. I would not only like to see this legislation through, but thrown out. I ask Liberal Members, since they did not speak, to vote against this legislation and show the people of this country that they will not take the bread out of the mouths of the children.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again, I think the Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) always manages to find

February 8, 1983
Family Allowances Act, 1973
the right word to express his sentiments. However, he should be careful not to let his eloquence become pure rhetoric. I think all Members of this House want family allowances to be granted to those who need them. I also believe that this Government has always preferred to grant family allowances on a universal, rather than a selective, basis. After listening to the Member for Bow River, I feel that his rather unusual approach may give the impression that the present Government intends to remove family allowances, a measure aimed at helping families by providing them with a supplement so that their children can get an education and have a decent standard of living. It is perfectly normal and legitimate that Members on both sides of the House should try to safeguard a measure that was introduced after a long struggle, namely, the family allowance, to ensure that families get the maximum benefit.
However, I believe that for the information of the House, 1 should perhaps point out that the difference between what would have been given under full indexing, and what will be given with indexing capped at 6 per cent, is not more than $1.40 per child per month. The fact that the previous speaker made such a big issue of this merely goes to show that he is overly fond of dramatizing the situation. Certainly, it would have been more attractive to grant full indexing, and even more, to the families that need it most, but if the tax burden is to be shared by all Canadians more or less equitably, it was necessary to find a way to help all Canadians get out of the recession without undue difficulty, so that the 6 and 5 program as applied to family allowances is just as fair as when it is applied to old age pensions or all public service employees. In addition, many provincial governments and private enterprises have adopted the same measure to fight the effects of inflation.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage, it is important to make the point that if we succeed in bringing the inflation rate down from 12 to 9, from 9 to 6, and then to 5 and 3 per cent, the 6 and 5 program will automatically cease to exist. What really matters is not the six and five program. The important thing is to bring inflation down to zero, because the six and five program in itself is meaningless unless we intend to reduce inflation gradually down to nothing. One important fact-and 1 am convinced that my colleague opposite will agree with me-is that Canadian families want to see an end to inflation, mindless of the six and five restrictions. They are hoping that our economic system will be rid of inflation once and for all. That is important.
Hon. Members opposite should stop dramatizing in this House and wasting hours in needless debates on this Bill, because they are not helping the Government of Canada and the people in our ridings. As I said earlier, an amount of $1.40 per child will be deducted from the monthly allowance cheque, and that will work out to about $13 a year. But there is something else which may be even more significant since family allowances help a family meet its expenses. 1 am referring to the child tax credit, something which the Hon.
Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) and some of his colleagues could have mentioned.
The child tax credit was implemented three years ago and it will not be affected by this Bill. To enlighten Hon. Members, I would add that the child tax credit enables a family to save $400 per year per child, non taxable, in addition to the family allowances mentioned earlier. In my opinion, the tax credit is basic, quite valuable and more important even than the family allowances. Hon. Members might be interested to know that two thirds of our Canadian mothers are entitled to the child tax credit which enables their families to get that additional assistance from the Government.
When Hon. Members opposite say that this Bill is totally unfair to families, and histrionically claim that we are depriving those families of much needed social benefits, I think they are on the slippery slope towards demagoguery and ought to be more careful. Naturally, the ideal solution would have been to let Canadian families enjoy full indexation and provide them with as much help as possible. As in anything else, however, expectations are unlimited, but the ability to pay is limited indeed. That is why we have to make a choice. I think that anyone in this House who honestly looks at this measure and makes a non-partisan judgement on it will readily admit that justice is being well served. The only thing that might be said is that it would have been desirable to have full indexation, but even if we had agreed to that, families and workers in Canada would have been worse off in the long run. In an economic system undermined by inflation, which year after year is eroding the purchasing power and boosting prices to the extent that each month families are faced with higher prices for food and clothing, I think that if the rates were to stay at 20, 12 or 14 per cent, the first who would unjustly be most affected are those we want to protect today.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that when you really think about it, the Government has no alternative but to cut back the so-called full indexation of benefits which we have had for four years and which have caused prices to nearly double in eight years and played havoc with our economy. If we compare Canada with some other industrialized countries, we realize that their action is perhaps much more drastic than ours because they are trying to completely abolish family or social assistance. If we look at the extremely drastic measures proposed by the United States and at the action taken in Germany and even in France, it is very easy to see that the action taken here does not come near what has been done in other industrialized countries of the free world. These are the things we should consider instead of trying to make political gains over a reduction of $1.40 per child in the basic amount of family allowances. I believe that the complementary legislation which will provide a non-taxable tax credit of $400 per child for two-thirds of Canadian mothers more than compensates for the $1.40 which each family will lose every month per child because of the six and five program.

On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, if we look to the future, we can see that the six and five program will, in the long term, provide more purchasing power for the goods which a family needs. Moreover, Canadian families will then have full value for their money, and this is what Canadian men and women have been asking for two or three years. They want to have once more a balanced purchasing power based on the income generated by their wages and industries. As a matter of fact, this is the real problem in Canada. We cannot simply say that because of some piece of legislation a certain group in our society will temporarily be deprived of a minimum amount compared with another group. What is important is to know whether this minimal amount represents less than the income which people will have because our economic system will no longer be affected by inflation. In other words, what is important is to determine whether a child tax credit of $400 a year really represents a purchasing power of $400 and whether these $400 are worth more than $500 because with $500, people can only purchase goods for a real value of $350 or $400. That is the problem of inflation we face at the present time. It is this inflation the Government is trying to fight in an effort to put more money in the pockets of Canadians than there is at the present time. Otherwise, inflation will increase and everyone will lose more every month and every year.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, my speaking time being very limited, I simply want to invite Hon. Members to support this Bill because, in the long term, it will be of benefit to all Canadian men and women.

increments. We are at the point where the amounts become very small.

We are one of the few Government which has not really cut back in social services in any significant way. The last time I spoke on one of these Bills, 1 mentioned that the President of the United States, President Reagan, went to Houston in June. He spoke to 3,500 people who paid $1,000 a plate for lunch. At the same time, the State of Texas was putting out a brochure saying that no one should come to Texas for welfare because they would get $34 in food stamps and $34 in welfare a month. That is not the kind of Government we have in this country, and I do not want to see that happen. Yet, I hear some rumblings among the neo-Conservatives, the Reaganites around this country, that that is precisely what should happen.
Family Allowances Act, 1973
We in this Party had a major debate on that subject at our last convention. We were almost unanimously in favour of universality on all of these subjects and in favour of maintaining the Family Allowances across the board. I believe it is important that we maintain social services in this country in a full way. These are the real issues in this debate.
There is a segment in our population, and I do not deny them their right to speak, of those who would abolish these things, who would like to get us back to a medical system similar to the one in the United States. I believe that that argument is one which we must continue to keep in front of us. We on this side of the House believe very strongly that universality is a basic right of Canadians. The Family Allowance is part of that, as is the old age pension and our public medical services, and so on. These are the kinds of things which we will defend. In spite of the fact that we have a recession and a large deficit, we have not in any material way cut back in those services.
I am very concerned about the direction in which we are all moving and I feel impelled very strongly to talk about how we can spend a good deal more money than we are spending on the services as well as on creating jobs to make sure that Canadians are able to afford the basics of life. It seems to me that at this stage we have to begin to pay a lot more attention to the kind of rhetoric which we hear about our deficit being a dreadful thing and how the economy is going to be destroyed by such large deficits, and so on. I would remind you of a recent study carried out by the University of Toronto Institute of Policy Analysis which looked at our deficit, and this is what people are complaining about in terms of social services. The study showed that our deficit is a short-term, not a structural, deficit. They took the recession out of the economy and found that without a recession we would have a small surplus, about $1.2 billion this year. On the other hand, a similar kind of study on the American economy would show the deficit was in the order of $60 billion to $90 billion after you remove the recession. Therefore, if this is a short-term deficit, a recession deficit, most of it caused by declining revenue and not so much by Government spending, then it appears to me at this stage of the game it should not be a reason for not going ahead and spending large amounts of money in job creation. I am talking about $6 billion, $8 billion or $10 billion. I would suggest this has to be short-term spending, not long-term, so it does not become a part of a permanent structural deficit. The last speaker from the Government side, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae), devoted most of his deliberations today to the issue of universality. Before I heard him speak, I had already planned to comment about that because yesterday the Minister, in speaking to her motion for time allocation, seemed to launch into a tirade against the Official Opposition on the issue of universality. Both I and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin), and perhaps others, have in the past tried to teach her a few lessons about plain, ordinary English-I dare say even French, too-and the meaning of the word "universality". I dare say there is no difference in either language. The Minister has a somewhat bizarre understanding of what universality actually means. Of course, she is torn between the divergent and mutually exclusive concepts of universality on one side, and her desire to help those who need it most on the other side. But it is absolutely impossible to have both at the same time. There is just no way. As you read the Minister's speeches from day to day, or even on the same day, you will find her saying first one thing, and then advocating the opposite.
As an example, before she got very far into her speech on time allocation on Bill C-132 yesterday, she accused the Official Opposition of wanting to abolish the concept of universality. Let me at this point establish the definition of universality, Mr. Speaker. According to the Oxford Concise Dictionary, universality is something applicable in all cases. Well, at the present time most of the Government's programs are not applicable in all cases. The Guaranteed Income Supplement, which is becoming a greater part of the Old Age Security system, becomes less and less a universal program because it takes over a greater proportion of the payments made to the elderly. The same is happening in the Family Allowance program where the Minister, by cutting the Family Allowance component of the total contribution made to
families, is moving further and further away from what used to be the concept of universality. But the Minister refuses to recognize that.
Let me use universal suffrage as an illustration. I am sure the Minister would agree that the concept of universal suffrage is something that gives each person, male or female, one vote. When the Minister talks about universal social programs, she is not talking about everyone getting the same thing; she is talking about everyone getting perhaps $1, and then a decent amount being given to those who need it most. I am not arguing with the validity of helping those who need it most, but the Minister must not try to ride two horses at the same time because it is impossible to have a universal program and at the same time give the same benefits, as you do in universal suffrage, to the same people. It is just impossible, but the Minister does not seem to be able to grasp that at all.
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, after attacking us on the problem of universality, she said she was dealing with the issue of the importance of fighting inflation and the six and five program, this big marketing program we have been subjected to across Canada. In discussing the first objective of fighting inflation the Minister said, and I quote from page 22572 of Hansard:
But we must not do this on the backs of those most in need, who in this case are the mothers.
But that is exactly what she is doing. Although she says she must not do it, she turns around and attacks the Family Allowance Program, the one progressive part of the total aid to families' program. This is just another indication of the duplicity and willingness to attempt to convey a message to Canadians about something which in fact is not being done through legislation of this Government.
One can go on and talk endlessly about a number of issues related to this Bill C-132 and its impact on families across Canada. It is affecting mothers and children in particular. It strikes out at the ones who are least able to defend themselves. It was pointed out to me a few minutes ago by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary West, that one aspect which has not been mentioned is the attack on families through the institutional care given to children who cannot be handled at home. This capping of the Family Allowance is going to affect all these institutions in Canada where children are housed because they receive these benefits. They are going to suffer a relative reduction in remuneration from the federal Government, and they are among the ones who can least afford it. Many of these institutions are in desperate straits now, and this will throw an added burden on them. It is just another example of the thoughtlessness of the Minister in attacking that part of society least able to defend itself. The situation has probably been most ably described by Terrance Hunsley, executive director of Canada Council on Social Development, who said before the Committee:
After 1983, in which low-income families will receive a one-time bonus payment of $50 per child, they will begin losing over $30 per child on a permanent basis and this loss is, in fact, indexed. In 1985, it will be about $36 per child-

The Minister seems to think there is some virtue in this Bill because it is going to help save money for the federal Government and therefore help in the fight against inflation. Well, the statistics seem to suggest about one twentieth of 1 per cent of total federal budget spending is going to be saved by virtue of Bill C-132, or something in the order of $10 million to $15 million. So it is very difficult to see how we are going to get any effective change in inflation as a result of this Bill.
In conclusion, I just want to say that when the Minister goes on the attack about universality, she forgets the words of Shakespeare when he said, "Methinks the lady doth protest too much".
