Mr. Speaker, I believe that this Bill, which will obviously pass through the House at third reading because it is now going through a time allocation procedure, will impose an economic hardship on many children in this country. I also firmly believe-and this happens to be the position of my Party since we believe in the concept of universality-that we will look back on this day as the day when the Government decided to do away with that concept of universality. That is exactly what this Bill does. It tampers with the original principle behind Family Allowances, that they shall be universal.
Of course, we know that Family Allowances were originally introduced to help offset the economic burden of raising a family and to help give people who were raising families some reasonable degree of equality of opportunity.
As one of my colleagues has already said, this Bill will also impose an unfair burden on some institutions in this country that care for children. For example, there is an orphanage in my constituency that cares for boys of all religious denominations. It is operated by the Order of Christian Brothers. This legislation will cause them serious problems because it will unfairly cut into their income. This happens at a time of serious downturn in our economy. They have seen their public support diminish by virtue of high unemployment, high inflation and the general deep recession which the country is presently going through. From all points of view, this is a mean, cruel and unfair Bill which should never have been introduced. Certainly it should never have been subject to time allocation or closure.
Let us look at the context in which this Bill was introduced. A few days ago, Statistics Canada released its unemployment figures. Those figures indicated that unemployment in Canada has risen by 100,000. There are now 1.6 million people officially unemployed in this country. When one takes into account the hidden unemployed, those who have given up hope of looking for a job, there are two million people unemployed in Canada in real terms.
My Province has the highest rate of unemployment. It is over 17 per cent. That unemployment problem, with all of its social implications, is compounded by the fact that the duration of the recession and the longevity of unemployment has meant that there are 100,000 unemployment recipients a month who are coming off UIC because their benefits have expired. Where do those people turn? They have no choice but to become subject to a means test and apply for welfare.
That is the context and time frame within which we are considering this Bill. Among the two million unemployed and the 100,000 who are coming off UIC benefits every month, I would suggest that it is not unreasonable to say that many would be heads of families. Again, this will erode their ability to care for their families. This is a mean and niggardly thing for this Government to do.
If I did not participate in the debate on this Bill, my conscience would bother me as, I am sure, the conscience of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) must be bothering her today. This Bill is not consistent with the social conscience that we recognize the Minister has and that she has brought to her portfolio up to now. I do not believe that she is at all happy about this Bill. I do not believe she is happy about doing away with the principle of universality. I do not believe that she is happy about the application of the six and five formula to this country's very important social benefit.
We may say that the amount of money concerned is not very much. Hon. Members can argue that it will be made up by the Child Tax Credit. However, many people will not qualify for the Child Tax Credit. Many lower and middle-income Canadians will not receive enough from the Child Tax Credit in the long term to make up for the loss in the Family Allowance benefits. What does this mean for unemployed people with large families? It means that their children may have to go without a pair of shoes. It means that their children may have to go without adequate clothing. In many instances it means that children in this country will have to go without an adequate diet. That is one of the consequences of long-term unemployment today and the expiration of unemployment insurance benefits. It is a consequence of the burden that has been placed on some of the poorer Provinces that have had an increase in the number of welfare recipients and decrease the benefits to some. There are many families that are facing hardship and are no longer able to cope in terms of being able to clothe their children adequately and provide an adequate diet.
February 8, 1983

The figures show that we still have double-digit inflation. Of course, the perverse argument would be put forward that this is the reason for the six and five formula. It will not hurt a Member of Parliament very much to hold him or her to a 6 per cent increase. As a matter of fact, 6 per cent of $100,000 amounts to a $6,000 increase. However, it becomes a very cruel act to hold a $26 a month Family Allowance benefit to that six and five formula. It means that the family will be deprived of the indexing that will allow it to offset the detrimental effects of inflation in a small way. The high cost of food, shelter, clothing and transportation which can be seen in the Consumer Price Index every month is what imposes the hardship on the people who have the burden of raising families today.
Quite frankly, I just do not understand the concept behind this Bill. I am ashamed that this Government would not only introduce this Bill but impose time allocation on it. Poor people have to pay inflated rates for clothes. Poor people have to pay inflated rates for footwear. Poor people have to pay taxes. We see taxes going up. Municipalities have had to raise property taxes, and those taxes are going up constantly.
In my Province the sales tax has risen from 11 per cent to 12 per cent. Sales taxes are going up in all Provinces across the country. Tuition fees are going up as well. Yet we hear the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) tell the young people of Winnipeg not to expect jobs this summer because of the slow progress in an economic turnaround. There will be hundreds of thousands of young Canadians coming on to the job market in April and May who will have no jobs or income to support themselves for another year of university or no way to offset the burden on their families because they could not get a job last year. That is the mess that has been created in this country.
I can understand the rationale behind trying to curb inflation by bringing expenditures under control. Perhaps at another time we can bring unemployment under control. The argument might even be made for capping indexing of Family Allowances. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the Minister that there is no argument that can support the introduction of this Bill at this particular time, because the reverse is true. Instead of bringing in a Bill to cap Family Allowances to six and five, we should be providing additional help to families that are faced with the burden of double-digit inflation, increased shelter costs, increases food costs, increased taxes, increased tuition fees and the additional burden of young kids not being able to find jobs to help finance their university and post-secondary education. I believe this is a cruel and an unnecessary bill. I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare should be ashamed of herself for bringing it in at this time.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to say a few words on the report stage of Bill C-132 dealing with Family Allowances, and especially on the amendment that we are now considering that has been proposed by the Flon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). It is also pleasant to follow the knight in shining armour who last spoke, the bearded avenger of the NDP. If there was a single word of truth in what he said, I do not think I would be able to live with myself. However, the facts of the case are somewhat different.
The amendment that we have before us today would in fact split the argument down the middle. The Government has come forward with a proposal to limit the indexation of Family Allowances for a period of two years. There have been many arguments presented which indicate that this may not be the correct thing to do. We know that we would be unsuccessful in defeating the Bill, but I think there is some chance of success for passage of the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Calgary West. It is a kind of compromise deal, and I would urge all Members of the House to vote in favour of that amendment.
We could live with the Bill, as we propose to amend it, for a year, and after that time we could assess the effect that the reduction in Family Allowance payments has had. If we feel that the reduction has not had such a deleterious effect as some people are predicting, we could continue in that vein; and if not, we could go back to full indexation. I would hope in the spirit of compromise that all Members of this House would vote for that amendment.
I, like other Members on this side of the House, am rather disappointed that the people on the Government side have chosen not to speak this morning or this afternoon. They spoke vehemently yesterday when the subject matter of debate was closure on the issue of Family Allowances. Having achieved that, having voted to close off the debate, they no longer seem interested. 1 do not think that they have advanced sufficient argument to support their point of view, and I was rather hoping that this afternoon we would hear arguments as to why, in their opinion, we should not vote in favour of the amendment. These arguments have not been forthcoming, and I rather suspect they do not exist.
Yesterday, while speaking on closure on this matter, I referred to the little guys who have been thrust out onto the firing line by the Government in the so-called fight against
inflation, whereas the Liberal fat cats have stayed behind the lines, at the back of the scene of action, and they have not been suffering at all on account of the Government's so-called six and five program.
Today we have seen another manifestation of that. It has come to light that, by Order in Council, the remuneration of the Hon. Donald Macdonald, who is heading the Royal Commission inquiring into the economy, is to be paid the exorbitant sum of $800 a day, and $925 a day when he is on the road. I do not buy at all the explanation given by the Prime Minister earlier in this House this afternoon when he said in fact that figure is only $400 because the other $400 goes to pay his office expenses. He could quit his law firm and he would still be making $800 a day. It is not necessary that the overhead expenses of his office be paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. That is just another illustration of the Liberal fat cats behind the lines who are not taking any cutbacks themselves, but passing those cutbacks on to the little guys at the front of the line.
I could mention also Michael Pitfield who is enjoying a nice paid holiday, and Ed Clarke, the architect of the National Energy Policy, who is enjoying himself in the south of France. There are all kinds of illustrations that can be given to underline that argument.
Apparently, the Parliament of Canada has over a number of years come to the conclusion that there is a need for Family Allowances. If that need exists, then I think it is only fair and honest that a system of full indexation be applied to those Family Allowances. I can remember the debate in this House a little over a year ago when a new budget was coming in and we were talking at that time about the indexation and there were suspicions on this side of the House that the Government was contemplating deindexation of programs such as this one and deindexation of certain aspects of the Income Tax Act and other taxation acts. At that time we had reassurance after reassurance after reassurance from the Government front benches that the Government was not considering any system of deindexation. It was not, in that budget, but a year later in comes the deindexation.
Even if partial deindexation was retained, as is proposed in this case, the value of the moneys granted by way of Family Allowances or any other scheme are very rapidly eroded. If the difference between the real rate of inflation and the indexed rate, as it is to be in this instance, is something like 4 per cent or 5 per cent, it will only take less than ten years, probably eight years, until the actual real value of those allocations has been halved.
We on this side of the House have consistently supported the idea of full indexation, whether it be applicable to the Income Tax Act or other acts, in calculating deductions against income, or whether it be in this form of payment. Without full indexation, this leads to the kind of political manipulation that we have seen before on the part of the Government. It brings in a program such as Family Allowances with an amount of money attached thereto that means something to people.

Because that amount does not keep pace with inflation and because it goes down, in real terms, that allows the Government at the time of the next election to come out with a great announcement that it is going to increase these payments. It is a way of buying votes without bringing in any real new program. We have seen that before with Family Allowances.
I remember a few years ago when the rate was $6 per month per child. Originally that was a reasonable amount, but it came to be worth very little. At that time the Government could have gone two ways. It could have got rid of the Family Allowance altogether. It would not have hit people very hard. On the other hand, it could do what it did at that time, come forward with a great increase to $20. I am sure that was done with electoral machinations in mind.
The Bill we are debating here today, C-132, will allow the Government to do precisely the same thing. It will allow them to engage in yet another publicity stunt at the time of the next election. If the Government was sure that the six and five program was going to work, and if it had done those things that are necessary to curb and abate inflation, if it had reduced its deficit, these measures would not be necessary because inflation would be less than 6 per cent and we would not have to cap it at that.
In closing, I should like to say that all Members of this House ought to support the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Calgary West and, if that fails, to go against Bill C-132.

control of the economy when we know that the opposite is actually the case. What burns me in this whole process of the Government, responding to political demand in the country that real action and real programs be to put in place straighten out the economy, is that it has followed a course which Governments have followed over the years. When entering into a program of restraint or restraining financial expenditure, they consistently aim their attacks at those least able to defend themselves.
We saw that in Bill C-131, and we know that the seniors of this country are not a politically organized group. They are not organized to the extent that they can fight back against that kind of restrictive measure. The Government did the same to public servants. Even Government spokesmen pointed out in this House that that was because the Government believed the public servants were not very popular in this country and therefore it was safe to attack and blame them.
We now have Bill C-132 where the Government in its assessment, and probably as a result of public polling, has decided that those who are recipients of the Family Allowance are not a highly organized group. They are not organized like the banks and the corporate sector. They fought very strongly against restrictions which the Government brought down in the infamous budget of a year or so ago. Because of their political strength, they managed to persuade the Government to change those elements in the budget which they felt were detrimental to their interests. The seniors of this country do not have that kind of clout with which to fight back.
The way the Government has brought this program in, it has convinced people that under the six and five program they will receive a monthly increase in any event and that the reduction will be extremely small, probably not noticeable. At the end of that two-year period, the reduction for recipients of the Family Allowance will be a lot more than the 50 cents a month which the Government has been trying to persuade Canadians is what they will lose as a result of this legislation.
In committee the Minister explained to Canadians the Government's position in introducing the six and five program. I wish to quote from the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs of December 7, 1982. The Minister said this:
The Government's philosophy in the Cabinet discussion, which is what you want to understand, was made like this: In the June budget, we decided we had reached the time where the psychological dimensions of the too-high inflation we were witnessing in Canada had to be recognized and dealt with by another psychological weapon, which was a sword-and I know the words might make you smile-a sword of a national campaign of solidarity of all Canadians, mobilizing all Canadians toward cutting in half the forecasted rates of inflation of 12 and 10 to 6 and 5. It was an arbitrary-to my knowledge-choice of common purposes for Canadians to try to embark all partners into, as I said-to mobilize all partners.
I fail to see how the Government can use the sword against the elderly and children of this country to fight inflation when everyone knows the facts. Figures from the Government's own agency, Statistics Canada, clearly show that those groups being asked to mobilize with swords, tanks and everything else the Government can dream up to launch the fight against

inflation are the very victims of inflation. The reason the Government is victimizing those people further can only be put down as crass politics, sadism.
When we take a look at this Bill, and I would like to refer to some written notes now, we find that under the provisions of this Bill, the Government expects to save-and that is their terminology,-$155 million over the two-year period, that is, $25 million the first year and $130 million the second year. It proposes to do this by limiting indexation of Family Allowances to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. Without the budget, Family Allowances would have been $358.44 for each child, which was $29.87 per month per child in 1983. However, under the provisions of this Bill, the amount will only be $342.24.
The Government contends that most families, in reality, will not lose any money because it is going to make up the difference by a one-shot increase in the refundable Child Tax Credit. However, Mr. Speaker, there are several problems with this logic. First, of the 3.6 million mothers who receive Family Allowances, about 2.5 million also receive the Child Tax Credit. This leaves 1.1 million families who will have their Family Allowances reduced with no compensation at all since they are not eligible for the Child Tax Credit. To qualify for the full credit of $343 per child, a family must have a taxable income of less than $26,330 per annum. For families above this income level, the total is reduced by five cents on every income dollar. For two-child families the credit disappears at the $40,000 level. For one-child families it disappears at $33,000. Even at this high income level, there are some women for whom the Family Allowance represents the only money they can call their own.
In conclusion, I would simply urge Hon. Members of the House to follow the advice of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women in their presentation to the Committee on Health Welfare and Social Affairs, that it behooves every Member of this House, Liberal as well as Tory and New Democrat, to vote against this measure when it comes up for a vote this evening and the final vote on Thursday.

There is also a general consensus and agreement that it would not be fair to apply assistance such as the Family Allowance system unfairly. There are some very serious consequences of the Minister's new measure to put limits on the indexation of old age pensions and Family Allowances. Low income families in the North find it very difficult to have their incomes reduced, even by S30 or $40 per month. Their resources are taxed to the limit already. The Hon. Member for St. John's East said that some children may have to go without shoes and without proper nutrition.
An even more serious impact of these measures is that people are losing their trust and confidence in this institution and in the Government. It is quite obvious that the Government has no intention of making a firm and unequivocal commitment to the contract we have entered into with Canadians. People are developing psychological barriers, saying, "If they can take that away from me now, what about my pension when I retire? Perhaps there is something in the fine print, and the Government will rearrange its priorities so that the pension will not be there for me when I need it." They are asking about unemployment insurance, saying, "I thought I would have it if I were ever laid off, but maybe the benefit can no longer be paid because the Government is running out of money. They have to pay Mr. Macdonald $300,000 a year to study the economy and perhaps buy some more service stations to ensure Canadian content in the energy sector of the economy. Perhaps there will be all kinds of different priorities." Certainly there is now doubt about the security and the legitimacy of the social contract we all thought we had arranged for people.
The damage done by the measures now before the House will probably never be corrected, Mr. Speaker. It is little wonder to me, and it should be little wonder to the Liberals, that people are becoming cynical about this institution and about the system we thought was fair and equitable for all Canadians, especially those in need. They become cynical about the political process and the promises and by politicians. They see that when it suits their political purpose, they default on those promises.
This is a very serious measure we are concerned with, Mr. Speaker. It places the whole process in question. We shall fight this measure with all the power we have-and it is precious little as you know. The Government has no qualms about closing off debate at any time in the House, saying, "We know what is best for Canada. We know what is right. You in the Opposition are just tolerated here." This institution no longer makes policy; it no longer has control of public spending, Mr. Speaker.
I should have liked to go into detail about how devastating this measure is for families on fixed incomes and families in the North where the cost of living is one and a half times or twice that of families in the more populated areas of the country. I should have liked to demonstrate what it means to people in the North who are paying a penalty for manning the frontier. Their children are deprived of the social amenities enjoyed in more organized areas of the country.

friends in the New Democratic Party to come to their senses before it is too late.
